Colonies of Broad-leaved hornwrack (Flustra foliacea) are among the most conspicuous bryozoans on sublittoral hard substrates in the northeastern Atlantic, forming erect, foliaceous fronds that often exceed dimensions typical of related flustrids. Maximum frond size is determined by colony age and local hydrographic conditions, with the ultimate total length of an individual zooid reaching 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], a measurement that reflects the species' capacity for sustained modular growth in environments with moderate to strong tidal flow. This growth habit produces broad, leathery lobes that provide structural complexity for a diverse epifaunal community. The colonial architecture of F. foliacea, built from closely packed autozooids, allows efficient water circulation across the feeding surface, a necessity given that each zooid captures suspended particulates via its lophophore. Morphometric studies of preserved specimens indicate that frond thickness and branch width increase proportionally with colony size, though these traits also exhibit plasticity in response to wave exposure.

Physiological rates in Flustra foliacea are strongly temperature-dependent, a relationship that constrains both growth and metabolic performance across its geographic range. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], researchers have documented a maximum lifespan of 4380 days [am = 4380 days], a longevity that underscores the species' slow, iterative mode of colonial development. This value, equivalent to twelve years, is notably high among temperate bryozoans and allows colonies to accumulate many generations of zooids over time. The annual growth check visible in some frond sections provides additional validation for these ageing estimates, as does the persistence of tagged colonies in long-term monitoring studies. Seasonal fluctuations in food availability and photoperiod interact with this thermal baseline to modulate feeding rates and metabolic costs, which in turn influence the pace of zooid budding and the eventual size of the frond.

At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], this developmental timeline allows young colonies to invest their first year's growth in skeletal infrastructure before shifting resources toward reproductive structures. The onset of sexual maturity marks a pivotal transition in the colony's energy budget, as the production of brooded larvae requires substantial investment in ovicell formation and larval provisioning.

Genetic and ecological factors further modulate the expression of life-history traits in Flustra foliacea, particularly along latitudinal gradients. Populations inhabiting warmer southern waters may experience accelerated development, though the specific influence of temperature on the duration to sexual maturation remains incompletely characterized. For individuals reared at a constant 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the attainment of puberty occurs within one year after birth [tp = one year after birth], a relatively rapid transition for a colony-forming gymnolaemate that continues to add zooids throughout its life. This pace of maturation is likely an adaptation to the seasonal predictability of phytoplankton blooms in temperate shelf seas, ensuring that larvae are released when food for the founding zooid is most abundant. Comparative studies with other flustrids from deeper or more polar waters would clarify whether the observed timing represents a conserved trait or a locally adjusted response to environmental regime.

The ecological role of Flustra foliacea extends beyond its own life cycle, as the complex three-dimensional matrix of mature fronds provides critical nursery habitat for juvenile invertebrates and demersal fish. A fully grown colony, having reached its ultimate total length of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], can host dozens of associated species within its fronds. The longevity of these colonies, up to 4380 days [am = up to 4380 days] when maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], permits the gradual accumulation of sediment and organic debris among the zooid rows, fostering a distinct microfaunal assemblage. This structural persistence contrasts with the shorter-lived foliose bryozoans that dominate disturbed shallows, emphasizing the role of F. foliacea as a foundation species in less impacted ecosystems. Continued monitoring of population age structure will be essential for predicting how warming seas may alter the species' distribution and the broader community dynamics it supports.
